newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Eastern Europe woos Singapore investors.
newsitem.headline: Eastern Europe woos Singapore investors.

text.p: Seven eastern and central European launched a drive on Tuesday to lure more Singapore investors into their emerging markets.

The Singapore Trade Development Board (TDB), which promotes foreign investment in Singapore and encourages firms to invest overseas, said Singaporeans had shown interest in manufacturing, trading, infrastructure and hospitality services.

The TDB will lead a trade mission of 15 to 20 Singapore firms in May to Poland, Slovenia, Hungary, Czech Republic, Bulgaria, Croatia and Latvia, the countries involved in a conference staged to launch the investment drive.
"We hope to highlight the business opportunities available and increase market transparency of the region," Barry Desker, TDB's chief executive officer told the conference.
Singapore's bilateral trade with eastern and central Europe has grown 200 percent since 1990 to Singapore $3 billion (US$2 billion) in 1996, Desker said.
Singapore's total investment commitment in the region has reached over S$500 million, mainly in real estate, manufacturing and warehousing, he said.
Bank Austria's Franz Horhager told the conference that potential investors should not venture into these markets alone.

"You need to be guided into these markets. Once you're guided, you can circumvent easily the traps, pitfalls, problems with local currencies and government regulations," said Horhager, the bank's director of international commercial banking and global networking management.

Horhager said he was optimistic about the investment advantages these former communist countries had over Asia's emerging economies like Cambodia or Burma, given their abundantly cheap, skilled labour force.
"In eastern, central Europe, people are skilled technicians, engineers. The percentage of academdic degree is extremely high. That's their main thrust," Horhager said.

Businessmen in the audience told Reuters they were wary about investing in the region due to a lack of knowledge on the various countries' politics, financial operations, legalities and business climate.
Horhager said such problems had eased in recent years.

"Things have calmed down since the breakdown of Soviet Union. Economic structures are in place with proper legal systems and new constitution. Problems are no longer characteristic of eastern Europe but how they are going to sell their products or get a good price," Horhager said.
"Most important is the countries' legal reliability. And that's the biggest achievements we have witnessed for the region," he said.
